title: Fed Official: Inflation Isn't Gone, Don't Bet on a 'Temporary' Rate Cut
dek: Goolsbee worries the economy is overheating: the inflation decline is mostly supply-side repair, services still show no effect; cuts below neutral need evidence, not front-running.
why: This episode features a rare clear self-account by Goolsbee: why he voted against last year, how he views AI investment and overheating, and the real changes at the FOMC under Warsh.
who: Traders and macro hedge fund researchers concerned about the Fed's policy path, as well as primary market practitioners trying to judge whether AI investment poses overheating risks.
skip: The opening R-star theory discussion can be fast-forwarded; the focus starts with the inflation decomposition and AI spillover sections.

points.h: If inflation stays above 3%, rates aren't tight
points.body: Asked whether current policy is restrictive, Goolsbee declined to answer directly. He said the key is the real rate, i.e., the nominal rate minus inflation expectations or actual inflation. His long-run landing point is 3% nominal, 2% inflation, 1% real. If inflation is above 3%, the real rate is much lower than it appears. He is willing to wait, but is nervous about the last six months of inflation data. This opening sets the tone for the whole episode: you can't discuss tightness without reference to inflation.

points.h: Saying 'wait three more months' every quarter isn't temporary
points.body: Goolsbee breaks down current inflation: tariff- and war-driven oil price spikes are one-off price level shocks that should fade, but he cautions from the COVID experience—a large enough supply shock can persist far longer than initial forecasts. What really worries him is services inflation, which is neither tariffs nor oil, and represents a deeper problem. His test: you can't say 'wait three more months' every quarter; he needs to see actual evidence of fading.

points.h: Stealing electricians isn't overheating; wage spillover is
points.body: On AI data center construction, Goolsbee says what he hears from Midwest businesses are complaints: data center operators buy up land, push up prices, and there are no electricians or HVAC workers. But he stresses that industry-level resource competition is not the same as economy-wide overheating. Only if AI investment pushes wages and prices beyond its own sector, lifting national unemployment and indicators beyond GDP, would it count as traditional aggregate demand excess. If it gets to that point, current policy is not restrictive enough.

points.h: Two-thirds of this inflation cycle came from supply, not demand
points.body: Looking back at the aggressive 2022-23 rate hikes, Goolsbee gives a ratio: roughly two-thirds of this cycle's inflation rise and fall came from supply, one-third from demand. He credits the Fed for ensuring 'the other shoe didn't drop': TIPS breakevens stayed stable at 2.3% even as CPI approached 10%, showing the 2% target anchor held. He admits the Fed was slow to start, but insists you can't have it both ways—you can't blame stimulus for the rise and credit supply chain repair for the fall.

points.h: 5.25% long-end yields aren't a credit panic
points.body: On rising long-term Treasury yields, Goolsbee says time is needed to distinguish drivers: it could be inflation expectations, market expectations of sustained high rates, or increased issuance supply. He rejects the 'market panicking about US credit' interpretation, because if there were genuine default concerns, 5.25% yields would be historically normal. He quotes Volcker: the Fed acts, the market reacts; the order can't be reversed. Market signals can inform, but the market shouldn't tell the Fed what to do.

points.h: The dot plot isn't a reaction function; the median isn't from one person
points.body: Goolsbee separates forward guidance from reaction function. He opposes forward guidance that 'commits to a rate hike or cut at a specific meeting,' as it ties hands and increases volatility. But markets need to understand how the Fed views economic data—that's the reaction function. The problem with SEP and the dot plot: the median inflation and median rate don't necessarily come from the same person, so the dot plot can't truly serve as a reaction function. He says he's opposed to SEP for years because members write down forecasts and get burned later, hurting credibility.

points.h: Without evidence of inflation fading, don't cut early
points.body: He gives his own reaction function: highly attentive to the inflation side; if he sees inflation genuinely declining toward 2%, he's willing to return to the '3-2-1' path; if especially services inflation is still rising with no progress, he gets nervous. He explains his dissenting vote late last year: with the government shutdown and missing data, he was uncomfortable front-running a cut without evidence, not wanting to act on the assumption that 'inflation will disappear on its own.' This explains his divergence from the current majority.

points.h: Powell only moved a few seats; the FOMC has shifted gears
points.body: Asked how a Warsh-chaired FOMC differs from the Powell era, Goolsbee says his personal feeling is very different. The new chair's demeanor at press conferences, worldview, and willingness to revisit communication tools all differ; Powell is still on the committee, just moved a few seats over. He won't comment on the chair's personal reaction function, saying everything will have to wait for the verbatim minutes four years and nine months from now. For listeners, this signals the Fed is in a transition period, and market speculation about the reaction function will continue.

terms.def: The theoretical real neutral rate that measures whether monetary policy is restrictive; not directly observable.
The Fed's quarterly compilation of members' forecasts for inflation, unemployment, and rates; the dot plot is part of it.
A central bank's communication pre-committing to a future rate path; Goolsbee thinks it was needed at the zero lower bound but should be reduced now.
The rule by which a central bank responds to economic data; Goolsbee stresses it is not the same as a specific rate commitment.
An empirical rule mapping inflation and output gaps to a suggested rate; at the zero lower bound it once suggested negative rates.

quotes.text: I always called our star our Sasquatch and you know somehow it feels with this as a backdrop because you can never see it until after it was left
It has to get out of its lane of just direct competition and drive up wages, drive up prices outside of just its lane.
I wasn't there when it went up, so you can't blame me.
Paul Volcker used to tell me, our job is to act and the market's job is to react and let's not get the order mixed up.
The reason I dissented in the last meeting of the year when they cut rates was I'm not comfortable front loading the rate cuts, counting on this inflation to be transitory and go away.

If inflation is going to be persistent, then it's going to force action by the Fed or by any center. If it's going away on its own, or if you even feel like it could go away on its own, then. It puts us in a very different circumstance.
